I've put together a list of a few things beginners might want to avoid when buying their first real (non-childhood) bicycle. Those considering their first adult bike purchase who don't want to spend a lot of money may find some of it useful.

  • Plastic parts - Plastic doesn't play well with bicycles. Even if it works when new, it will eventually dry out and crack, every time. So avoid a bike with plastic brake handles or plastic anywhere else where it is stressed while riding. You don't want levers made of plastic. You don't want plastic on your derailers or brakes. That being said, even the best parts will often have some plastic incorporated into them -- but they won't be load-bearing parts that are stressed. Also, carbon fiber is not plastic -- two different things.

  • Built-in rear derailleur hanger - You don't want to buy a bike that does not have a separate, removeable rear derailleur hanger. Some cheaper bikes have the derailleur hanger as an extension of the frame, and if it gets damaged, as they often do, it cannot be replaced because it is part of the frame. Sometimes you can bend it back into shape, but often you cannot, and then you are screwed.

  • Steel wheels and/or spokes of common steel - Steel wheels are heavy and eventually rust. Wheel spokes of common steel will eventually rust. Spokes of ordinary steel are also subject to galvanic corrosion when used on an aluminum rim (you will recognize this because the rust on the spoke is right at the end of the spoke, where it enters the aluminum rim). You want aluminum rims and stainless steel spokes.

  • Carbon wheels with rim brakes - Rim brakes generate heat, and heat degrades carbon fiber. Too many people have had their carbon wheels fail because they were using rim brakes -- avoid this combination. Disk brakes are not a problem with carbon wheels.

  • Chinese no-name carbon frames, wheels, handlebars and seat posts - Not all carbon is the same. When you buy no-name carbon from China, you are rolling the dice with your life. When carbon fails, it fails catastrophically.

  • Fixed gear or coaster bike - This may be disputed by some riders, but a beginner should avoid the temptation to go the cheaper and simpler route by buying a fixed gear bicycle, unless they live in a completely flat region such as Florida. You need gears to climb hills, and you need them more when you are a beginner.

  • Full-suspension mountain bikes - Beginners will not be skilled enough to take advantage of a rear suspension. By that I mean they will not be able to handle the kind of downhills that require a full suspension. Full suspension bikes are heavy and perform poorly on ordinary paved or gravel roads. Plus, good-quality rear suspensions are expensive. When you are looking for a cheap first bike, it is much better to go with no suspension at all, or with a front-suspension hard-tail mountain bike.

  • No-name components - Buy major brand name derailleurs and shifters. Buy brand name brakes. Avoid derailleurs, shifters and brakes with no brand name at all, and avoid unknown brands which are often the same as no brands. Shimano is always a good name to buy. So are SRAM and Tektro.

  • Avoid Amazon and department store bicycles - They are tempting because they are so cheap, but there is a reason they are cheap. Often they are not built strongly enough to actually ride for any distance before they fall apart. And when they do break, as they always do, it is sometimes impossible to get replacement parts. Only buy from the larger bike brands such as Trek, Giant, Cannondale, Specialized and so on. You won't find these brands in department stores or on Amazon.

  • In general, avoid second-hand bikes older than ten years or so - The technological advances in bicycles have been significant over the past decade. There is no need to saddle yourself with obsolete tech when you buy your first bike. Get something reasonably recent, and it will be easier to ride and easier to fix.
